### Observed differences

- Work on A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was reallocated between resources. In the earlier window, each of these activities was spread over many resources with no dominant performer — the most frequent resource handled roughly 7–13 in 100 executions, and a long tail of occasional resources covered about half of all executions. In the later window, a largely different mix appears: User_3 became the most frequent performer of every one of these activities (about 11–15 in 100, up from about 3 in 100 or less), User_78 entered the top group at about 6–9 in 100, and several previously frequent resources dropped out or fell to small shares. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]

- A11 moved from shared to single-resource handling. Earlier it was spread over 23 distinct resources, with the most frequent of them (User_100) performing about 15 in 100 executions; in the later window, every observed execution of A11 was performed by User_100 alone (top-resource share 100 in 100, concentration index 0.06 to 1.0). [ASSIGN003, CONC001]

- How often the affected activities occurred stayed essentially stable — A01 appears in all 200 traces in both windows, A11 in 111 of 200 earlier and 102 of 200 later traces — so the difference lies in who performed the work, not in how often the activities ran. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

- Out of A10, successor choices were redistributed: transitions to A16 fell from about 57 in 100 to about 44 in 100, transitions to A07 rose from about 10 to about 24 in 100, and transitions to A11 fell from about 17 to about 11 in 100. [DIR001]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that resource allocation changed in the later window. For A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, execution shifted from one group of resources to a largely different group, with User_3 and User_78 among the main gainers and several previously frequent resources losing most of their share; in addition, A11 changed from being distributed over about 23 resources to being performed exclusively by User_100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

The supporting signs are direct and consistent: the resource family produced 8 qualifying items where about 0.006 would be expected by chance across the 12 units tested, far beyond what an unchanged process typically produces; each difference is larger than in about 999 of 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data; the redistribution runs in the same direction across all seven activities; stable activity occurrence rules out an activity-frequency explanation; and the concentration measure independently confirms the extreme single-resource handling of A11. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]

Limitations: resource codes are anonymous, so nothing can be said about roles or teams behind them; A13 and A14 show identical profiles and may reflect one shared behaviour rather than two independent changes; and the evidence cannot distinguish one overall reallocation covering all these activities from separate per-activity changes. [ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005]

Other differences: the redistribution of successor shares out of A10 described above. This is the only control-flow item, in a family where about 0.2 items are expected without change, so it falls within the range an unchanged process typically produces and does not by itself establish a structural change. [DIR001]
